scope: Four original, mock-eligible AQA Physics Electricity 3.5.1.2/3/5/6 written diagram and practical application questions, separate from flashcards.
notes: These are entirely original exam-style educational questions, not official past-paper items or official mark schemes. All require independent human marking of actual diagrams and working. Practical scenarios are reported-data analysis rather than directions to conduct experiments. No existing card IDs, answers, scores or profile data are changed.

questions.subtopic: Complete ohmic-conductor, filament-lamp and semiconductor-diode I–V sketches
questions.question: Draw and compare three complete current–voltage characteristics
questions.prompt: On THREE separate axes with current I/A vertical and potential difference V/V horizontal, sketch the characteristic curves for (a) an ohmic resistor at constant temperature, (b) a filament lamp for both positive and negative potential differences, and (c) a semiconductor diode including ordinary reverse bias. Label each curve. Explain why the resistor is ohmic and why the lamp resistance rises as its potential difference grows in magnitude. [8 marks]
markPoints: Label current I/A on each vertical axis and potential difference V/V on each horizontal axis, with each origin correctly located.
For the constant-temperature ohmic resistor draw a straight line through the origin with positive gradient in both positive and negative quadrants.
Explain that, for the ohmic conductor under constant physical conditions, current is directly proportional to potential difference.
For the filament lamp draw a continuous curve through the origin that becomes less steep as the magnitude of voltage increases.
Show the filament-lamp curve in both positive and negative quadrants, with the physically corresponding sign of current.
Explain that the lamp filament gets hotter, increasing its resistance, so I does not rise in direct proportion to V.
For the diode show negligible current in its normal reverse-bias region, rather than a symmetric ohmic line.
For the diode show a small initial forward current followed by a rapid forward-current rise as forward voltage becomes sufficient, without assuming one universal exact threshold.
questions.modelAnswer: I/A is on each vertical axis and V/V on each horizontal axis. The ohmic resistor has a straight positive-gradient line through the origin in quadrants I and III: I ∝ V at constant temperature. A filament lamp passes through the origin, with the slope dI/dV decreasing as |V| increases in both polarities: the hotter filament has greater resistance. A normal semiconductor diode gives negligible reverse current over ordinary reverse bias and appreciable forward current only after a forward-voltage region, then increases steeply. Check the student's three actual curves, their quadrants and their axes; words alone cannot earn drawing marks.

questions.subtopic: RP5 resistivity circuit, R–L gradient, area and uncertainty
questions.question: Interpret a complete required-practical-5 resistivity report
questions.prompt: A school laboratory report investigates the resistivity of a uniform wire using low-voltage measurements. (a) Draw and label a circuit showing the wire section, ammeter and voltmeter in their correct positions. (b) Explain how wire length, diameter, current and potential difference would be recorded and how the R-against-L graph would be used. A sample report gives R=1.60 Ω at L=0.400 m and R=3.20 Ω at L=0.800 m; wire diameter d=(0.500±0.010) mm. (c) Calculate gradient, area and resistivity with units. (d) Estimate percentage uncertainty in the area from diameter alone and explain how graphing helps with possible contact resistance. This is analysis of a reported practical, not a request to carry it out. [10 marks]
markPoints: Draw or describe the measuring circuit with the ammeter in series with the test wire and the DC source.
Place the voltmeter in parallel across only the measured length of wire, not across an unrelated component.
Specify measuring wire length and multiple micrometer readings of the diameter along the wire and at more than one orientation, obtaining a mean diameter.
State that R=V/I is found for several measured lengths and R is plotted on the vertical axis against L on the horizontal axis.
Convert d=0.500 mm=5.00×10⁻⁴ m and use A=πd²/4.
Calculate A≈1.96×10⁻⁷ m².
Use ρ=(gradient)×A to obtain ρ≈7.85×10⁻⁷ Ω m.
Diameter has 2% percentage uncertainty, giving approximately 4% uncertainty in area from the diameter squared.
Explain that using an R–L best-fit gradient distinguishes slope from an additive lead/contact-resistance intercept; temperature control is important because the wire resistance changes with heating.
questions.modelAnswer: The ammeter goes in series with the low-voltage source and measured wire; the voltmeter goes in parallel across the selected wire length. The report should measure L, take several micrometer diameter readings and use the mean d, calculate R=V/I for several lengths, and plot R (Ω) versus L (m). Using the sample points, gradient=(3.20−1.60)/(0.800−0.400)=4.00 Ω m⁻¹. d=5.00×10⁻⁴ m, so A=π(5.00×10⁻⁴)²/4=1.9635×10⁻⁷ m². Since R=ρL/A, resistivity is ρ=(4.00)(1.9635×10⁻⁷)=7.85×10⁻⁷ Ω m. The diameter fractional uncertainty is 0.010/0.500=2%; because A∝d², the area contribution is about 4%. A nonzero R-axis intercept can arise from connecting leads/contact resistance; the R–L gradient helps separate that additive term. Heating should be controlled or minimised in any supervised experiment. Inspect the diagram and actual working before awarding marks.

questions.subtopic: Draw two NTC/LDR potential-divider sensor circuits and prove output directions
questions.question: Design and analyse two sensor potential-divider diagrams
questions.prompt: Consider two separate ideal 10.0 V DC potential dividers, each containing one fixed resistor and one sensor. Draw labelled circuit diagrams with supply polarities and Vout terminals. (a) Design an NTC-thermistor divider whose Vout increases when temperature rises. (b) Design an LDR divider whose Vout decreases when light intensity increases. In each case justify the output direction using the correct expression for the potential difference across the lower component. The diagrams are to be assessed on paper. [8 marks]
markPoints: Draw both dividers as two components in series across the supply and label the 10.0 V supply polarity.
For the NTC circuit, place NTC in the upper branch and the fixed resistor in the lower branch, with Vout across the fixed lower resistor.
State that raising temperature decreases NTC resistance.
Use Vout=10.0×Rfixed/(RNTC+Rfixed) or an equivalent divider argument to show that the NTC circuit output rises.
For the LDR circuit, put the fixed resistor above and the LDR in the lower branch, with Vout across the lower LDR.
State that increasing light intensity decreases LDR resistance.
Use Vout=10.0×RLDR/(Rfixed+RLDR) or an equivalent divider argument to show that the LDR circuit output falls.
Label each Vout measurement correctly between the junction and the bottom/negative terminal, rather than an unrelated point.
questions.modelAnswer: Both designs have a fixed resistor and a sensor in series across the 10.0 V supply. For rising output with temperature, place the NTC thermistor ABOVE the fixed resistor and take Vout across the LOWER fixed resistor: Vout=10.0Rfixed/(RNTC+Rfixed); temperature up makes RNTC smaller, so Vout rises. For falling output with increased illumination, place the fixed resistor ABOVE the LDR and measure Vout across the LOWER LDR: Vout=10.0RLDR/(Rfixed+RLDR); brighter light makes RLDR smaller, so Vout falls. On both sketches label the supply positive at the top, negative at the bottom, and Vout between the central junction and the lower terminal. Actual circuit topology, polarity and measurement points require manual checking.

questions.subtopic: RP6 emf/internal-resistance circuit, V–I graph, gradient and lost volts
questions.question: Analyse a full required-practical-6 terminal-pd report
questions.prompt: A report on a cell gives two points from a straight-line terminal-pd V against current I plot: (I=0.20 A, V=1.42 V) and (I=0.80 A, V=1.12 V). (a) Sketch a labelled circuit diagram with the cell, adjustable external resistor, ammeter and voltmeter to explain how paired I,V data would be obtained. (b) Sketch an appropriately labelled V-against-I graph and use V=ε−Ir to obtain its gradient, internal resistance and emf. (c) Calculate the lost volts at 0.20 A and state one reason for using multiple readings and a best-fit line. This is analysis of a supplied report, not instructions to perform an experiment. [9 marks]
markPoints: Draw the cell, adjustable external resistor and ammeter in one series loop.
Put the voltmeter across the cell's external terminals, with the measured terminal pd clearly indicated.
Explain that changing the external resistance yields a sequence of paired current and terminal-pd readings.
Put V/V on the graph's vertical axis, I/A on its horizontal axis, and indicate a decreasing straight-line best fit.
Use V=ε−Ir, identifying vertical intercept ε and slope −r.
Infer internal resistance r=0.50 Ω, not −0.50 Ω.
Calculate ε=V+Ir=1.42+(0.20×0.50)=1.52 V and lost volts Ir=0.10 V at 0.20 A.
Explain that multiple readings and a best-fit line reduce the effect of random scatter and make intercept/gradient estimates more reliable.
questions.modelAnswer: The ammeter and adjustable external resistance are in series with the cell; the voltmeter is connected across the cell's external terminals. The report obtains paired I and terminal V values for different external resistances. For the V-against-I graph V is vertical and I horizontal. Since V=ε−Ir, gradient=−r=(1.12−1.42)/(0.80−0.20)=−0.30/0.60=−0.50 V A⁻¹, so r=0.50 Ω. The vertical intercept is ε=1.42+(0.20×0.50)=1.52 V. Lost volts at 0.20 A are Ir=0.10 V. A set of readings with a best-fit line supports a more reliable intercept and gradient than relying on only two noisy measurements. The graph, actual connections, signs and units must be reviewed manually.
